strengths: RefAV targets an important and underexplored problem: retrieving a described multi-agent driving scenario while localizing its participants in 3D and time. The inclusion of negative queries distinguishes it from most referential-tracking datasets and makes log-level retrieval evaluation possible.

Building on Argoverse 2 provides synchronized cameras, LiDAR, maps, diverse object classes, and nominally 10 Hz tracks. The benchmark output—temporally delimited 3D tracks—is more actionable for autonomy testing than a text-only answer.

The paper provides several complementary baselines and separates perception from language-grounding effects using ground-truth-track oracles. RefProg substantially improves over the strongest same-tracker alternative: with LE3DE2E, HOTA-Temporal rises from 19.2 for RefBlind and 17.2 for RefClassify to 50.1.

The program-synthesis approach is modular and interpretable. Its API, prompts, tracking post-processing, multiple tracker backends, LLM ablation, sampling-rate ablation, and related-object results provide useful starting points for future work.
The authors recognize important limitations, including API coverage, perception-label noise, runtime, and the limited scale and diversity of the underlying driving logs.
weaknesses: The benchmark and principal method are strongly coupled. Of 10,000 expressions, 9,880 are procedurally defined by first composing the same hand-designed atomic API that RefProg later uses to reconstruct programs. Thus the large RefProg advantage partly measures inversion of the dataset-generation process, rather than general scenario understanding. Results are not separated between the 120 independently authored examples and the procedural subset, nor by seen versus novel compositions.

The central claims about natural, diverse, safety-relevant queries are insufficiently validated. Nearly all queries are LLM-generated, but the paper does not report annotator counts, independent annotation, agreement, rejection rates, or a quantitative semantic-error audit. Manual inspection is described, yet its exact coverage and protocol are unclear, especially for negative examples.

The benchmark specification is incomplete. No explicit train/validation/test sizes or rules for separating logs, prompts, programs, and near-duplicate compositions are given. This creates potential leakage for future learned methods and prevents assessing compositional generalization. The stated 8,000/2,000 positive-negative construction also conflicts with the appendix counts of 7,910/2,090 without explanation.

The evaluation undercuts the emphasized benefit of 10 Hz annotation: Appendix A states that final outputs are downsampled to 2 Hz for evaluation, and the sampling ablation shows only a 0.5-point ground-truth HOTA-Temporal difference between 10 Hz and 2 Hz. The paper therefore does not demonstrate that its main results require the claimed fine temporal resolution.

The broad conclusion that current VLMs perform poorly is not adequately supported. RefClassify deliberately crops each object without relational or temporal context, while RefInflate operates largely frame by frame. No contemporary video/multiview VLM, 3D grounding model, or adapted learned RMOT method receives the full scene and temporal context, so these experiments establish limitations of the selected pipelines rather than VLMs generally.

Several metric and data details need greater precision for reproducibility. HOTA-Temporal and HOTA-Track are described only verbally rather than formally; operating-point selection is unclear; RefClassify computes a prompt-specific top-10% threshold using scores across positive and negative dataset examples, which may use evaluation-set distribution information. Standard HOTA values for the same trackers also differ across Tables 2, 4, and 5 without a sufficiently clear account of the evaluated subsets.

There are internal data-description inconsistencies: the main text says every object track is clipped at 50 m, whereas Figure 7 says RefAV contains referred objects up to 150 m. Such ambiguity materially affects the task definition and difficulty.

Program synthesis itself is an incremental application of established visual-programming ideas, and the paper provides no uncertainty estimates, repeated LLM trials, sensitivity to in-context examples, or statistical testing. Minor writing issues—such as the missing Section 4.4, duplicated words, and Qwen model-name inconsistencies—are presentation refinements rather than decision-determining concerns.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important computer-vision problem: retrieving and spatiotemporally localizing planning-relevant interactions in long, multimodal autonomous-driving logs.
RefAV adds useful task elements that many referring benchmarks lack, including 3D tracks, 10 Hz annotations, temporal action boundaries, related-object labels, and negative query-log pairs.

The modular RefProg baseline is technically sensible and obtains substantial gains over the reported alternatives: with LE3DE2E tracks it reaches 50.1 HOTA-Temporal versus 19.2 for RefBlind and 17.2 for RefClassify. Results with ground-truth and several predicted trackers help separate grounding errors from perception errors.

The manuscript includes multiple metrics, several perception backbones, an LLM ablation, a sampling-rate study, and useful implementation details. The main exposition and system diagrams are generally clear.
weaknesses: The benchmark and proposed method are circularly coupled. Of 10,000 expressions, 9,880 are procedurally defined from the same 28-function API that RefProg receives at evaluation time. RefProg is therefore largely solving the inverse of the dataset-generation process. Its large advantage may measure recovery of a shared latent program and generator style rather than general scenario understanding.

The paper provides no decisive evaluation on genuinely independent language. Only 120 expressions are manually defined, yet performance on these examples is not reported separately. There is also no evaluation with human-written queries, paraphrases, unseen compositions, held-out atomic functions, or an external dataset. Consequently, the claimed ability to mine naturally described scenarios is weakly supported.

The dataset validation protocol is insufficiently documented for a benchmark contribution. The manuscript says generated programs and videos were manually verified but does not report the number or qualifications of annotators, independent redundancy, agreement, rejection/correction rates, or a quantitative audit of temporal and object-label accuracy. The diversity-sampling objective is likewise undefined.

The experimental comparison does not substantiate the broad claim about current VLM limitations. RefInflate uses GroundingDINO and SAM, while RefClassify applies CLIP to isolated per-frame crops; neither is a strong temporal multimodal VLM. No contemporary video-language or multimodal-LLM baseline is evaluated, and RefProg itself does not reason directly over RGB or LiDAR but over precomputed tracks and hand-engineered geometric functions.

The evaluation construction is unclear and potentially too easy. Positive pairs are produced by executing programs on all logs, whereas negatives are randomly sampled; there is no analysis of hard negatives differing by one relation, action, or temporal condition. Exact log/query split construction is not specified, making it difficult to assess leakage between similar prompts, programs, and scenes.

Several central evaluation details are under-specified. HOTA-Temporal and HOTA-Track are described informally rather than defined precisely, and there is no category-, scenario-, or composition-level breakdown, uncertainty estimate, or significance analysis. Aggregate results can therefore conceal severe failures on rare safety-critical interactions—the stated motivation of the work.

Reproducibility from the manuscript is incomplete. The appendix provides API signatures and docstrings rather than implementations, and omits exact data splits, the diversity-sampling procedure, annotation-quality statistics, runtime/cost, and some selection/tuning details. Dependence on proprietary Claude models also makes exact reproduction time-sensitive.

The writing has noticeable but mostly non-material presentation problems, including numerous typographical errors, inconsistent terminology and coloring, a missing Section 4.4, and some table/reference inconsistencies. These should be corrected, but they are secondary to the benchmark-validity concerns.

strengths: The paper formulates a practically important and underexplored vision problem: retrieving natural-language-described driving events while localizing the relevant objects in 3D and time. Requiring negative-query handling and precise tracks makes RefAV more useful than conventional referring-expression or scene-level VQA benchmarks for safety-oriented log mining.

RefAV is a potentially valuable benchmark contribution: it provides 10,000 query-log pairs over 1,000 multimodal Argoverse 2 logs, includes 2,090 negative examples, exploits 10 Hz annotations, and covers object motion, map context, multi-agent relationships, weather, and lighting.

The empirical results establish that the task is nontrivial and that language grounding, rather than tracking alone, is a major bottleneck. For example, evaluating all ground-truth tracks gives only 13.3 HOTA-Temporal, while RefProg reaches 64.8 with ground-truth tracks and 50.1 with LE3DE2E tracks.

RefProg is a sensible, interpretable baseline. Its decomposition of prompts into executable geometric and temporal predicates is well matched to compositional driving queries, and its 50.1 HOTA-Temporal substantially exceeds RefBlind (19.2), RefClassify (17.2), and RefInflate (4.0) under the reported settings.

The evaluation separates temporal grounding, whole-track localization, log retrieval, and timestamp retrieval through HOTA-Temporal, HOTA-Track, and balanced-accuracy metrics. Results with several perception backbones and five LLMs provide useful evidence about where performance is lost.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes unusually extensive implementation information, the atomic-function interface, oracle experiments, related/other-object evaluation, a sampling-rate study, dataset statistics, and candid discussion of runtime and coverage limitations.
weaknesses: The most important limitation is circularity between benchmark generation and the proposed baseline. Of the 10,000 expressions, 9,880 are procedurally defined from the same atomic-function vocabulary that RefProg is asked to reconstruct. Consequently, the large RefProg advantage partly measures recovery of the benchmark's latent program grammar rather than general scenario understanding. Manual verification can improve label correctness but does not remove this structural advantage. Performance should be reported separately on the 120 independently authored examples, although that subset is presently too small for a definitive comparison.

The dataset validation protocol is insufficiently documented for a benchmark paper. The manuscript says generated programs and videos were manually verified, but does not report the number or expertise of annotators, independent redundancy, agreement, rejection/correction rates, or a quantitative audit of temporal boundaries and negative examples. This is material because the labels inherit thresholds, noisy tracks, and semantic definitions from hand-designed predicates.

The train/validation/test organization is not clearly specified: split sizes, whether prompts or program templates overlap across splits, and how test annotations are protected are absent. Template-level leakage could make evaluation considerably easier even for zero-shot prompt-to-program systems and would limit future supervised use of the benchmark.

The evidence for broad claims about off-the-shelf VLMs is narrower than the framing suggests. The evaluated alternatives are GroundingDINO/SAM inflation and crop-level CLIP classification; no contemporary video or multimodal LLM baseline directly reasons over the camera sequence, LiDAR, and map. Thus, the experiments convincingly expose weaknesses of these particular adaptations, but not VLMs generally.

Several design choices lack sensitivity analysis or independent justification, including the 50 m clipping distance, RefClassify's dataset-level top-10% threshold, 1.5-second temporal dilation, track-confidence truncation, and various atomic-predicate thresholds. These choices can materially affect both labels and measured localization performance.

RefProg's 64.8 HOTA-Temporal even with ground-truth tracks reveals substantial language-to-program or API-coverage error. The paper identifies weather and lighting as unsupported cases but does not break performance down by expression type, complexity, positive versus negative query, manual versus procedural origin, or rare versus frequent scenario. Such analysis is important for assessing actual safety-oriented usefulness.

Reproducibility is promising but not fully demonstrated within the manuscript: it refers generically to GitHub and Google Drive without visible URLs, while proprietary, versioned Claude and Gemini services are central to generation and evaluation. Exact decoding settings, repeated-run variability, API cost, and end-to-end runtime are not reported.

Presentation issues are secondary but noticeable: the claimed three contributions are not cleanly enumerated, Section 4.4 is missing, Table 5 appears to contain a citation mismatch for the 2 Hz Valeo4Cast row, and the paper alternates between 2 Hz output evaluation and emphasizing 10 Hz ground truth in ways that could be explained more clearly.

strengths: RefAV addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: retrieving and temporally/spatially localizing language-described multi-agent events in long, multimodal driving logs. The combination of negative queries, 3D tracks, HD maps, and 10 Hz annotations is potentially valuable to vision and autonomous-driving research.

The benchmark construction involved meaningful effort: 10,000 log-query pairs over 1,000 Argoverse 2 logs, manual inspection and correction of generated scenario definitions, and additional manually annotated interactions, weather, and lighting conditions. The paper also provides useful dataset statistics and concrete annotation examples.

RefProg is simple, modular, and empirically effective. With LE3DE2E tracks it obtains 50.1 HOTA-Temporal versus 37.2 for the GPT-5 black-box baseline and 20.2 for ReferGPT. Results across several trackers, ground-truth-track oracles, five LLMs, and 2 Hz/10 Hz inputs help separate perception, temporal sampling, and language-to-program effects.

The manuscript is generally clear and unusually detailed about implementation: it reports prompts, atomic-function documentation, post-processing, model versions, program failure rates, inference costs, and representative successful and failed programs. The nuPrompt experiment supplies some evidence that the compositional approach transfers beyond RefAV.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation is strongly coupled to the proposed method. Of the 10,000 pairs, 9,880 are labeled by programs composed from the same atomic-function family supplied to RefProg. Even though those labeling programs were manually checked and differ from RefProg's unverified generated programs, this shared representation can substantially favor RefProg. Performance should be separated for procedurally defined versus independently annotated scenarios; the latter comprise only 120 pairs and are too limited to validate broad real-world scenario understanding.

The claimed scale and diversity need qualification: the 10,000 entries contain only 407 unique descriptions, and 7,910 are positive pairs sampled from program matches. Thus this is primarily a benchmark of repeated log-query matching within a relatively small, predefined ontology, rather than 10,000 distinct natural-language queries. The narrow ontology also conflicts somewhat with broad claims about safety-critical scenario mining, as acknowledged by failures on weather, lighting, visibility obstruction, and other concepts absent from the API.

Independent evidence for RefProg is not fully controlled. In the nuPrompt comparison, RefProg uses StreamPETR while competing rows use different decoders such as PETR, PETRv2, or DETR3D, so the reported AMOTA gain cannot be cleanly attributed to referential program synthesis. No matched-backbone comparison or breakdown isolating the base tracker's contribution is provided.

Dataset reliability is not quantified. The paper reports roughly 200 annotation hours and manual verification, but does not state the number of annotators, independent double annotation, agreement, or a held-out annotation error audit. Since descriptions can be underspecified and program semantics define precise temporal labels, manual inspection by the same construction pipeline is insufficient evidence for annotation consistency.

Evaluation protocol details remain ambiguous despite the extensive appendix. The manuscript mentions validation and test sets and evaluates 150 test logs, but does not clearly specify all split sizes, whether unique descriptions overlap across splits, or where thresholds and post-processing constants were selected. Expression overlap is especially important because RefProg generates one program per unique description.

The custom HOTA-Temporal and HOTA-Track metrics are explained intuitively but not defined formally enough in the manuscript to verify edge cases. Several presentation issues also impede interpretation, including the confusing 'Ground Truth' label for the all-tracks oracle and unresolved challenge/code link placeholders. These are secondary to the benchmark-coupling concern but reduce clarity and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important problem: retrieving and temporally/spatially localizing planning-relevant interactions in large autonomous-driving logs. Requiring negative-query handling and 3D tracks makes the task more realistic than conventional referring-expression benchmarks.

RefAV adds potentially useful annotations to 1,000 Argoverse 2 logs, including 10 Hz tracks, multi-agent relationships, temporal extents, weather, and lighting. The examples cover interactions that are more relevant to driving than many attribute-focused RMOT queries.

The empirical study includes several baseline families, multiple 3D trackers, oracle-track experiments, five LLMs, cost statistics, failure examples, and a sampling-frequency ablation. RefProg's improvement over the matched black-box LLM baseline is substantial (50.1 versus 37.2 HOTA-Temporal with LE3DE2E tracks).

The program-synthesis framework is modular and interpretable: generated programs can be inspected, executed over track and map data, and debugged more readily than an opaque end-to-end prediction. The appendix provides prompts, API documentation, examples, and meaningful failure cases.
weaknesses: Material: The benchmark and principal method are circularly aligned. Of 10,000 examples, 9,880 are procedurally defined using 28 hand-designed atomic functions, and RefProg receives essentially the same function API at evaluation time. Consequently, its strong result primarily demonstrates recovery of benchmark-generating programs from their paraphrases, not general scenario understanding. The manuscript acknowledges the reversed generation direction but does not evaluate an independently annotated subset at useful scale, an unseen-function or unseen-scenario split, or a mismatched API that would establish generalization.

Material: The dataset is described as containing 10,000 diverse natural-language queries, but it has only 407 unique scenario descriptions; the remaining count represents log-description pairs. This substantially narrows the claimed linguistic and semantic scale. Only 120 examples are manually defined, leaving too little independent evidence to validate the broad scenario-mining claims.

Material: Dataset quality is insufficiently quantified. Positive examples are found by executing generated definitions, while negative pairs are sampled from their non-matches. The paper reports manual review and editing but gives no annotator count, agreement, independent audit, residual error estimate, or clear evidence that negative pairs were visually checked. Imperfect or underspecified programs can therefore create false negatives, directly affecting the balanced-accuracy metrics.

Material: The manuscript does not clearly specify how logs and unique descriptions are divided among training, validation, and test sets, whether descriptions overlap across splits, or how numerous thresholds were selected. Thresholds such as the top-10% similarity rule, 0.63 ReferGPT cutoff, motion thresholds, and temporal dilation could materially affect results. There are also no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite claims of significant improvement.

Material: The nuPrompt result does not support the claimed state of the art under a controlled comparison. RefProg uses StreamPETR, whereas reported competitors use DETR3D, PETR/PETRv2, or stereo decoders. Without an unfiltered StreamPETR tracker and matched-backbone baselines, the improvement cannot be separated from the stronger perception model.

Material: The evaluation does not include key controls for the proposed contribution: performance of the original generating program as an oracle, RefProg with a separately designed API, held-out atomic functions/compositions, or performance restricted to the 120 manually created examples. These controls are necessary to determine whether RefProg generalizes beyond the ontology embedded in the benchmark.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on changing proprietary models and services, while several evaluation metrics are defined only informally. The precise computation domains for log/timestamp balanced accuracy and the full mathematical definitions of HOTA-Temporal and HOTA-Track are not provided in the manuscript.

Presentation: The submitted PDF contains unfinished placeholders and broken prose, including an incomplete contribution sentence, literal “challenge” and “here” link text, and missing challenge wording. Some table values and tracker HOTA numbers also vary across tables without adequate explanation. These are correctable presentation problems, but they reinforce the manuscript's unfinished state.

strengths: RefAV formulates a practically important and underexplored problem: retrieving natural-language-described driving interactions while localizing the relevant objects in both 3D space and time. This is meaningfully different from conventional referring tracking and scene-level VQA.

The dataset leverages 1,000 Argoverse 2 logs with 10 Hz tracks, HD maps, LiDAR, and surround cameras. The inclusion of negative query-log pairs and temporally delimited referred tracks supports both retrieval and localization evaluation.

Dataset construction includes substantial quality control: generated scenarios are executed against tracks, positive clips are manually inspected, incorrect programs or descriptions are corrected, and manually designed scenarios supplement the procedural set. The reported annotation effort of roughly 200 hours is credible evidence of curation.

RefProg is a sensible, modular baseline that converts language into compositions of interpretable motion and spatial primitives. With LE3DE2E tracks, it raises HOTA-Temporal from 37.2 for the black-box GPT-5 baseline to 50.1, and the ground-truth-track result of 64.8 helps separate grounding limitations from perception errors.

The experimental analysis is unusually broad for a benchmark paper: it compares several grounding strategies, multiple base trackers, five code-generating LLMs, positive/negative retrieval metrics, related-object performance, inference cost, and temporal sampling rates.

Zero-shot evaluation on nuPrompt provides useful evidence that the proposed primitives are not wholly specific to RefAV. The method reports 0.321 AMOTA versus 0.259 for the strongest listed PromptTrack configuration.

The appendix supplies prompts, post-processing details, threshold values, annotation tooling, examples of both successful and failed synthesized programs, and the complete atomic-function interface. This supports understanding and potential reproduction.

The manuscript is generally clear, well motivated, and visually effective. It also candidly discusses failure modes such as insufficient API expressivity, invalid generated programs, perception noise, and the limited scale of AV2.
weaknesses: The principal scientific concern is construction-method bias. Of 10,000 query-log pairs, 9,880 are procedurally defined and there are only 407 unique descriptions. Their annotations are generated using compositions of the same 28-function API later supplied to RefProg. Manual verification improves label correctness but does not remove this structural alignment, which likely favors RefProg over methods without access to the benchmark-generating ontology.

The claim of 10,000 'diverse natural language queries' overstates linguistic diversity: most entries repeat one of 407 descriptions across logs, while only 120 examples are manually defined. Results should therefore be interpreted primarily as performance across query-log pairs rather than 10,000 independent language concepts.

The nuPrompt comparison does not cleanly isolate the contribution of RefProg because it uses StreamPETR, whereas listed competitors use DETR3D, PETR/PETRv2, or stereo inputs. Without a StreamPETR-only tracking baseline or applying RefProg to matched detector outputs, the claimed state-of-the-art generalization cannot be attributed solely to the language-grounding method.

Several decision rules are hand specified, including confidence filtering, similarity thresholds, majority voting, a 50 m relationship cutoff, and 1.5-second temporal dilation. The manuscript does not clearly state how these values were selected or whether test performance influenced them, limiting the strength of the quantitative comparison.

The stochastic LLM experiments appear to use a single generated program per description and provide neither repeated-run variability nor uncertainty estimates. This is especially relevant because failure rates vary from 0.5% to 18.1% and model/API behavior can change over time.

RefProg primarily reasons over precomputed tracks and maps rather than raw multimodal observations. It therefore establishes a strong modular baseline, but does not fully substantiate broader claims about multimodal VLM understanding; attributes such as weather and lighting remain explicit failure cases.

Reproducibility depends on proprietary, versioned LLM APIs, including Claude, Gemini, and GPT-5. The detailed prompts and token accounting help, but exact replication may remain difficult without released generated programs, cached outputs, split definitions, and evaluation artifacts.

There are presentation defects that should be corrected but are not acceptance-determining: missing or malformed challenge/GitHub links, incomplete sentences around the competition contribution, and some terminology/model-name inconsistencies. More importantly, the main text should state the dataset splits and threshold-selection protocol explicitly.
